notes.meaning: David promises Shimei that he will not be put to death and confirms it with a solemn oath. Having received forgiveness and restoration from God, the king chooses to show mercy to an enemy on his day of triumph. His oath protected Shimei from execution during David's own lifetime.

Saul's grandson Mephibosheth comes to greet David in a state of complete neglect. He had not washed his clothes, cared for his feet, or trimmed his facial hair since the day David fled from the city. These were outward signs of deep mourning that proved his ongoing loyalty to the king.

When Mephibosheth meets the king, David asks why he did not flee into exile with him. David had previously believed Ziba's report that Mephibosheth stayed behind to reclaim Saul's throne. This question gives Mephibosheth the opportunity to clear his name.

Mephibosheth explains that his servant Ziba deceived him. Because he was crippled in both feet, he had ordered his donkey saddled so he could ride with the king. Instead, Ziba took the supplies and left him behind without any way to travel.

Mephibosheth reveals that Ziba slandered him to make him look like a traitor. Even so, he praises David's great wisdom, comparing the king to an angel of God who can judge what is right. He humbly submits himself to whatever the king decides to do.

Mephibosheth admits that Saul's whole family deserved death under the rule of a new king. Instead of punishing him, David had shown him great kindness by welcoming him to the royal table. Because of that undeserved grace, he feels he has no right to demand anything more from the king.

David stops any further debate and decrees that Mephibosheth and Ziba must divide the family land. This effectively restored the first arrangement, where Ziba farmed the land and shared the harvest with Mephibosheth. While some see this as a fair compromise, others view it as a hasty settlement that left Ziba unpunished for his lies.

Mephibosheth responds by telling the king that Ziba can keep all the property. He cares far more about David's safe return to Jerusalem than about his own wealth. His unselfish reaction proves that his devotion to the king was sincere.
Barzillai, an elderly leader from the region of Gilead, travels down to escort David across the Jordan River. He comes out of deep respect to honor the king and send him safely on his journey home.

Barzillai is eighty years old and very wealthy. During David's desperate stay at Mahanaim, Barzillai had generously supplied food and resources for the king and his army. His practical generosity had kept the royal camp alive during the rebellion.

David invites Barzillai to cross the Jordan and live with him in Jerusalem. He wants to repay his friend's kindness by providing for him at court. This offer granted Barzillai a permanent place of honor beside the king.

Barzillai politely declines the king's generous offer. He asks how many years of life he has left to justify moving to the capital city. He recognizes that court life makes little sense for someone near the end of his days.

Barzillai explains that his age has dulled his senses. He can no longer savor fine food and drink, nor can he enjoy court music or serve the king effectively. Rather than enjoy royal luxuries, he does not want to become an added burden to David.

Barzillai explains that he only intends to walk a short distance past the Jordan with the king. He views his past service as simple duty rather than something requiring a lavish reward. True loyalty gives freely without expecting personal gain.

Barzillai asks permission to return home so he can die in his own town and be buried beside his parents. Instead of himself, he offers Chimham, widely understood to be his son, to cross over and receive the king's favor. He asks David to do for the young man whatever seems best.

David readily accepts the arrangement and promises to take Chimham with him. He assures Barzillai that he will care for the young man and grant whatever Barzillai asks on his behalf. The king gladly transfers his gratitude to the next generation.

The people and the king complete their crossing of the Jordan River. David embraces Barzillai with an affectionate kiss and a parting blessing before the old man returns home. This warm farewell shows deep mutual love and honor between the monarch and his faithful friend.

David moves forward to Gilgal accompanied by Chimham. All the men of Judah and half the forces of Israel form an escort for the king. Gilgal was the historic site where Saul had first been made king, making it a symbolic place for David's kingdom to begin anew.

The leaders of the northern tribes of Israel arrive and confront David. They complain that the men of Judah took the king away secretly and brought his household over the Jordan without them. They feel excluded and slighted by not being invited to participate in the restoration.

The men of Judah defend themselves by explaining that David is their close relative from the same tribe. They insist they did not take action for personal profit, free food, or special royal gifts. They acted quickly out of tribal loyalty and family affection.

The northern tribes argue that having ten tribes gives them a far greater claim on the king. They complain that their early support for bringing David back was ignored, but the men of Judah respond with even harsher words. This bitter argument exposes tribal rivalries that would eventually split the nation in two.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Traditional Catholic commentary notes that the real population difference between the two sides was nowhere near ten to one, making the northern claim to superior honour unreasonable.
